title: Atlas of Questions
premise: Opening slice: follow records, arguments and mathematical texts from a Babylonian teaching collection through Greek and Arabic investigations of light. These five chapters are dated reconstructions, not a universal origin story. Their numerical cases and dialogue are authored.

items.label: Clay tablet
items.description: A prepared writing surface for a short teaching account.

items.label: Reed stylus
items.description: A writing tool; making a mark does not establish that its content is true.

items.label: 12 + 18 measures
items.description: The teaching store received 12 measures, then 18 measures.

reading.text: The store received 12 measures of grain in the morning and 18 in the evening. The account concerns grain measures, not a count of jars.
reading.attribution: Authored arithmetic dossier; inspired by cuneiform accounting, not a translated tablet.

items.label: Grain, not jars
items.description: The account must distinguish measures of grain from numbers of containers.

items.label: Seen / clouded / missed
items.description: Dated reports distinguish a seen event, an obscured sky and a missed watch.

reading.text: Watch 1: the event was seen. Watch 2: cloud hid the relevant part of the sky. Watch 3: no observer was present. “Not seen” has three different evidential meanings here.
reading.attribution: Authored observational dossier, not a Babylonian quotation.

items.label: Date signs
items.description: Month and day labels attach a report to a time rather than a remembered story.

items.label: Earlier eclipse intervals
items.description: A small reconstructed series shows recurrent eclipse opportunities, not an eclipse at every opportunity.

reading.text: This deliberately simplified teaching series lists several recurring eclipse opportunities. Some events were seen; some were obscured. The intervals suggest another watch, but neither a clear sky nor an eclipse is guaranteed.
reading.attribution: Authored schematic series; not an authentic Babylonian algorithm or calendar.

items.label: Omen interpretation
items.description: A separate inherited interpretation links a celestial sign to affairs on earth. Recording and divination were not mutually exclusive.

reading.text: The same celestial event may appear in a record of what happened and in an interpretation of what it means for a ruler or city. Mesopotamian observation and divination were not mutually exclusive activities.
reading.attribution: Historical paraphrase of the research scope in Rochberg; no ancient words quoted.

items.label: Marked tablet
items.description: The surface now holds distinct marks. Their meaning still depends on units and context.

items.label: Number account
items.description: 12 + 18 gives 30 in this teaching account. Written calculation can be checked after the speaker leaves.

items.label: Reckoning table
items.description: The entry says 30 measures, not 30 jars. Explicit units make a numerical comparison meaningful.

items.label: Dated sky record
items.description: Observation and missing observation remain distinct. A cloudy night is not evidence that nothing happened.

items.label: Interval table
items.description: Counting dated intervals makes recurrence inspectable; no cause has yet been established.

items.label: Cycle table
items.description: Earlier reports support recurring eclipse opportunities. This simplified table is not a transcription of a Babylonian algorithm.

items.label: Watching calendar
items.description: The calendar identifies a time to watch and leaves room for an event to be absent or hidden.

items.label: Record and interpretation
items.description: The recorded event and its omen interpretation remain distinguishable, without pretending ancient observers excluded religious meaning.

items.label: Every dimming = cover
items.description: Speaker A: every observed darkening is caused by a covering body. The form and the premise can be tested separately.

reading.text: Speaker A: “Every darkening is caused by a covering body. This is a darkening. Therefore a body is covering the light.” The observed case and the universal premise are different claims.
reading.attribution: Fictional teaching speech, not Aristotle’s dialogue.

items.label: Inference form
items.description: If every A is B, and this case is A, this case is B. The example is a modern explanatory rendering of deductive form.

items.label: Same result, rival cause
items.description: Speaker B predicts the same darkening from a different mechanism; matching one observation does not choose between them.

reading.text: Speaker B proposes a different mechanism but predicts the same darkening at the same time. Agreement with this one prediction will not distinguish the two mechanisms.
reading.attribution: Authored logic case; not a historical claim that these speakers existed.

items.label: Dimming without cover
items.description: A dimming with no predicted covering challenges the sweeping word “every”; this is an invented counterexample.

reading.text: A recorded dimming occurs when the proposed covering body is absent. If the record and classification are accepted, the unrestricted claim “every darkening is a covering” fails.
reading.attribution: Authored counterexample, not an actual ancient observation.

items.label: Dark ≠ covered
items.description: The speakers alternate between “looks dark” and “is physically covered.” These are not identical descriptions.

items.label: Stated premises
items.description: The observed case is separated from the general causal claim. Neither can silently stand in for the other.

items.label: Valid argument
items.description: The conclusion follows if its premises hold. Validity alone does not establish the general premise.

items.label: Counterexample
items.description: The supplied case defeats the unrestricted claim. One failed claim does not prove every rival explanation.

items.label: Rival prediction
items.description: Both accounts can match this predicted event. A successful prediction is evidence, not a unique causal verdict.

items.label: Unsettled cause
items.description: The same outcome follows from different accounts; more discriminating evidence is needed. This is a modern reconstruction of the problem.

items.label: Distinct claims
items.description: An event report, an interpretation and a proposed mechanism answer different questions. Distinguishing them is not banning any of them.

items.label: Qualified claim
items.description: The revised claim says exactly which class of cases it covers, rather than retreating into an ambiguous word.

items.label: Open question
items.description: Which further observation would separate the rivals? The page ends with a real disagreement rather than a compulsory winner.

items.label: Straightedge
items.description: Draws a straight line; it cannot by itself certify every geometric claim.

items.label: Compass
items.description: Transfers a distance and draws a circle in the Euclidean construction.

items.label: Line segment
items.description: A given segment AB. The task is to construct an equilateral triangle.

items.label: Copy A: missing reason
items.description: A teaching copy preserves the two-circle construction but omits a justification.

reading.text: Witness A names a segment AB, two circles centred on A and B, and their intersection C. It says the three sides are equal but omits the reason. The witness is invented.
reading.attribution: Authored textual witness adapting the structure of Euclid, Elements I.1; not a quotation.

items.label: Copy B: wrong label
items.description: A second teaching copy has the justification and a conflicting label. Neither is an actual ancient quotation.

reading.text: Witness B explains that the relevant sides are equal radii, but one copied label calls the intersection D rather than C. The disagreement must remain visible while an editor proposes a reading.
reading.attribution: Authored textual witness, not a surviving ancient manuscript.

items.label: Editorial signs
items.description: Marks distinguish a disputed passage from a supplied reading; the exact notation is modern.

items.label: Two intersecting circles
items.description: Circles centered on A and B use AB as their radius. An intersection supplies a candidate third vertex.

items.label: Triangle diagram
items.description: Joining the intersection to A and B makes a triangle. The drawing suggests equality; the definition of a circle warrants it.

items.label: Geometrical proof
items.description: Each relevant side is a radius of a circle of the same radius. The equalities justify the construction rather than relying on appearance.

items.label: Proof conditions
items.description: A skewed-looking sketch does not refute the definitions; a missing construction premise would. Separate drawing quality from the argument.

items.label: Variant table
items.description: The missing justification and conflicting label are kept side by side, not silently harmonized.

items.label: Restored diagram
items.description: The geometric construction identifies the likely label while the alternative remains recorded.

items.label: Marked reading
items.description: The supplied label is visibly editorial. A plausible restoration is not an untouched original.

items.label: Critical text
items.description: The text presents the proof with its conditions and marks the uncertain reading.

items.label: Proof roll
items.description: Readers can examine both the geometric reasoning and the textual disagreement. This is a teaching roll, not an invention claim for modern critical editions.

items.label: Syriac witness
items.description: A teaching witness helps compare a Greek mathematical passage with an Arabic rendering; routes differed by work and translator.

reading.text: Some Greek scientific and philosophical works reached Arabic through Syriac intermediaries; other routes differed. A mathematical translation must preserve what a term does in a proof, not merely its dictionary equivalent.
reading.attribution: Historical paraphrase; Greek Sources in Arabic and Islamic Philosophy, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

items.label: Arabic terminology
items.description: Candidate renderings of ratio, equality and figure need mathematical context, not just word substitution.

items.label: Indian numeral treatise
items.description: A separate mathematical tradition supplies decimal positional calculation, including a place-holding zero. It is not derived here from Greek geometry.

reading.text: In positional decimal notation the same digit has different values in 3, 30 and 300. A vacant position must be represented consistently. Indian arithmetic enters this workshop as an independent tradition, not an invention made from the Greek proof.
reading.attribution: Modern demonstration within a historical reception setting; not an al-Khwarizmi quotation.

items.label: Unknown + 5 = 12
items.description: A teaching payment has an unknown amount x plus 5 making 12. The notation x is modern.

reading.text: An unknown amount, with five units added, equals twelve units. The modern shorthand is x + 5 = 12. Modern notation is used to make the teaching case compact, not credited to the ninth-century manuscript.
reading.attribution: Authored algebra case, not a historical transcription.

items.label: x² + 6x diagram
items.description: A diagram represents x² + 6x. A 3 by 3 corner would complete the larger square.

reading.text: A square of side x has area x². Two strips, each of width 3 and length x, add 6x. Their arrangement leaves a 3-by-3 corner. All lengths in this geometric case are positive.
reading.attribution: Modern positive-magnitude illustration of square completion; not an unrestricted historical symbolic formula.

items.label: 3 × 3 missing corner
items.description: Adding the 3 by 3 corner also changes the other side of the equality.

items.label: Compared witness
items.description: The proof is checked across witnesses rather than credited to a single universal translation bureau.

items.label: Arabic proof
items.description: The translated geometric argument is intelligible and checkable; translation itself involves mathematical judgment.

items.label: Decimal procedure
items.description: The same quantities can be calculated with positional digits. Zero preserves a vacant place; it is not a claim that one culture invented all arithmetic.

items.label: Written equation
items.description: The account becomes x + 5 = 12 in our modern notation; the unknown is constrained instead of guessed.

items.label: Balanced operation
items.description: Removing equal amounts from equal amounts preserves equality. Subtracting 5 on both sides gives x = 7.

items.label: Checked solution
items.description: Substitution gives 7 + 5 = 12. A reversible step and a check make the answer more than an unexplained rule.

items.label: Square construction
items.description: The strips are arranged geometrically. The gap shows why a correction term is needed.

items.label: Completed square
items.description: Adding 9 turns x² + 6x into (x + 3)². The same 9 must be added to the other side.

items.label: Algebra method
items.description: Numerical checking and geometrical justification now accompany a reusable method. Al-Khwarizmi’s work is a development, not passive storage of inherited texts.

items.label: Lamp
items.description: A movable source of light, not a physical ray.

items.label: Opaque board
items.description: Blocks light except where an aperture will be made.

items.label: Small aperture
items.description: Selects a narrow bundle of light paths.

items.label: White screen
items.description: Makes arriving light visible. Stray illumination can wash out a faint projected image.

items.label: Bright courtyard
items.description: The upper doorway and lower paving can be distinguished in an image.

items.label: Two lamp positions
items.description: Two marked source positions permit a deliberate comparison without changing the aperture.

items.label: Aperture board
items.description: The board now admits a narrow set of paths instead of flooding the screen.

items.label: Image box
items.description: A screen faces the opening. The arrangement is still washed out unless the surrounding room is dark.

items.label: Camera obscura
items.description: In darkness an inverted image appears: upper and lower paths cross at the aperture. This demonstration is not an exclusive-inventor claim.

items.label: Ray diagram
items.description: Straight lines model light propagation in a uniform medium; a ray is a representation, not a luminous thread.

items.label: Crossed rays
items.description: Tracing paths through the opening explains the image inversion geometrically.

items.label: Predicted spots
items.description: The diagram predicts where light from each marked position should reach the screen.

items.label: Comparison record
items.description: The lamp is moved between the specified positions and the observed spots are recorded. This is a deliberate test of this arrangement.

items.label: Optical model
items.description: The same ray geometry accounts for the image and the moved-source observations. It does not settle all questions of vision.

items.label: Optical question
items.description: Light reaching an eye still needs an account of image formation and perception. A successful aperture demonstration is not the entire theory of sight.

locations.label: Dark room
locations.description: A context that makes a faint aperture image visible; place the receiving optical arrangement here.

sources.title: NASA/JPL: AEGIS autonomous science targeting
sources.note: Actual bounded target-selection autonomy. It is not evidence that the fictional self-questioning laboratory exists.

sources.title: Francesca Schironi: Textual Scholarship in Alexandria and Beyond
sources.note: Scholar-authored research on textual practices. Modern apparatus and translation terms in this game are not all ancient Alexandrian inventions.

sources.title: Oxford History of Science Museum: mathematics in Islamic cultures
sources.note: Practical problems, inherited mathematics and original contributions cross languages and regions. No exclusive origin claim.

sources.title: Influence of Arabic and Islamic Philosophy on the Latin West, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
Aristotle: Prior Analytics, translated primary text
sources.note: Ancient syllogistic; modern symbolic notation and toy examples are explanatory reconstructions.

sources.title: Francesca Rochberg, Science and Ancient Mesopotamia, Cambridge History of Science
George Boole: An Investigation of the Laws of Thought (1854)
sources.note: Primary historical text; binary gate notation is a modern teaching representation.

sources.title: Eduard Buchner, Alcoholic Fermentation Without Yeast Cells (1897), translated primary text
Eleanor Robson: Digital Corpus of Cuneiform Mathematical Texts
sources.note: Scribal arithmetic and numerical records; game quantities are invented, not translated tablets.

sources.title: Charles Darwin, Recollections of the development of my mind and character, manuscript autobiography, Darwin Online
Euclid: Elements, David Joyce edition
sources.note: Greek mathematical text in a modern explanatory edition. Diagram alone is not proof.

sources.title: From DNA to Beer, US National Library of Medicine
MacTutor: Leonardo Pisano Fibonacci
sources.note: Liber abaci (1202) and learning arithmetic in North Africa; not invention of Indian numerals.

sources.title: Ørsted compass needle, 1828 — Science Museum Group
sources.note: A surviving demonstration instrument, not a claim about a single dramatic discovery moment.

sources.title: Oersted’s experiment — Institute of Physics
sources.note: Supports opposite compass directions above and below a current-carrying wire. Construction and power-supply instructions deliberately excluded.

sources.title: Michael Faraday’s ring-coil apparatus — Royal Institution
sources.note: August 1831 apparatus and brief induced current in the other coil; object evidence anchors the reconstruction.

sources.title: John Graunt: Natural and Political Observations on the Bills of Mortality, 1662
sources.note: Primary text for population tabulation. Historical cause labels have uncertainty.

sources.title: Greek Sources in Arabic and Islamic Philosophy, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
Mark Schiefsky, The Creation of Second-Order Knowledge in Ancient Greek Science
OU primary-book exhibition: Harvey
sources.note: Harvey used quantitative, experimental, analogical and teleological arguments. Recipes isolate questions rather than reconstruct his whole reasoning.

sources.title: Siccar Point: geological evidence and Hutton
sources.note: Hutton used an unconformity to support an existing account of repeated geological processes; one scene does not establish every feature of his theory.

sources.title: Gysel: Vesalius’s Fabrica and the masticatory system
sources.note: Historical research contrasts the earlier Tabulae with the Fabrica’s account of a unified mandible. Adult anatomy; developmental fusion complicates an unqualified one-bone slogan.

sources.title: Museo Galileo: Kepler, Ad Vitellionem paralipomena
sources.note: Kepler revises inherited optics; telescope observation alone did not uniquely prove heliocentrism.

sources.title: Royal Museums Greenwich: Harrison and longitude
sources.note: Chronometers and lunar distances coexisted. Sea trials, cost and reproducibility matter alongside invention.

sources.title: Darwin Correspondence Project: Charles Lyell
sources.note: Documented geological influence with continuing disagreement, not blanket acceptance.

sources.title: Thomas Malthus: Essay on the Principle of Population, 1798
sources.note: The ratios are Malthus’s argumentative model, not a universal empirical law or moral instruction.

sources.title: Maths in the Early Islamic World, BBC synopsis reproduced by participant Peter Pormann / University of Manchester
Isaac Newton, General Scholium, 1729 English edition, Newton Project
NIST AI RMF Core
sources.note: Model validation, generalization limits and ongoing evaluation. A checklist is not a guarantee of trustworthiness.
